ThreatsDay: Game Cheat Spyware, 24-Hour Ransomware, Chrome Sync Stalking + 12 More Stories

The Hacker News
2026-07-16 23 use cases 13 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

A lot of this week’s trouble starts with something that looks close enough. A familiar repo. A useful installer. A harmless sync setting. Then the handoff goes bad, the box starts talking to someone else, and the damage moves faster than the explanation. Old bugs are back, weak defaults are earning their keep, and some attack paths are so plain they barely feel like research. Here’s the mess.

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Trojanized MobaXterm/WebEx/Zoom/DBeaver/FaceIT installer run from user path (UAT-11795) · [LLM] pepesoft.exe game-cheat surveillance payload dropped from pepegit666 GitHub/Hugging Face infra · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] SAM registry hive dump during rapid intrusion (Spirals ransomware) · [LLM] IIS worker (w3wp.exe) spawning shell/recon processes — ASP.NET web shell (Spirals ransomware) · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — ThreatsDay: Game Cheat Spyware, 24-Hour Ransomware, Chrome Sync Stalking + 12 Mo
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] curl.exe spawning PowerShell stager (UAT-11795 Starland RAT → WLDR agent) · Suspicious browser extension installation · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Spirals ransom note C:\RECOVERY_SECTION.log written to disk · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Crypto-wallet file/keystore access by non-wallet process · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft)
curl.exe spawning PowerShell stager (UAT-11795 Starland RAT → WLDR agent) AIInstallation High
Hunts the UAT-11795 execution hand-off where the Python-based Starland RAT invokes curl.exe to pull and run a PowerShell stager that decrypts the in-memory WLDR C2 implant. curl.exe as the direct parent of powershell.exe is aberrant on user endpoints and is the campaign's signature chaining step. Rationale: Talos states Starland RAT "uses curl.exe to execute a PowerShell stager for decrypting and running WLDR agent"; curl.exe-as-parent-of-powershell.exe is a rare, campaign-specific process-tree edge. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/uat-11795-deploys-novel-starland-rat-and-bespoke-wldr-c2-implant-in-financially-motivated-campaign/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/russian-hackers-trojanize-webex-zoom-apps-to-push-starland-malware/
ATT&CKT1105 T1059.001 T1218.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer scripts that pipe curl output into PowerShell for CI/build bootstrapping
  • IT automation using curl to fetch a .ps1 then invoking it
  • Package managers/installers that shell out to curl then PowerShell
  • Security tooling that chains curl + PowerShell for telemetry pulls
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("github.com","raw.githubusercontent.com") and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("install","bootstrap","choco"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the curl command line and the child PowerShell command line — look for a remote URL fetch feeding an inline/hidden PowerShell stager and any subsequent long-lived powershell.exe with no on-disk script. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the powershell.exe implant, and capture memory (WLDR is memory-only). 3) Hunt: pivot on the same DeviceId for a preceding mshta.exe/HTA launch and a trojanized installer (MobaXterm/WebEx/Zoom/DBeaver/FaceIT), and for outbound encrypted beaconing from powershell.exe.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "curl.exe"
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\\curl.exe"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\powershell.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\pwsh.exe"
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine

Trojanized MobaXterm/WebEx/Zoom/DBeaver/FaceIT installer run from user path (UAT-11795) AIDelivery Medium
Hunts the UAT-11795 initial-access lure: trojanized installers masquerading as MobaXterm, WebEx, Zoom, DBeaver, or FaceIT delivered via ClickFix/HTA and executed from Downloads/Temp/AppData rather than a vendor-signed install path. Anchors on the campaign's specific decoy software set plus a script/browser launcher parent. Rationale: Talos names the exact decoy set (MobaXterm, WebEx, Zoom, DBeaver, FaceIT) delivered via ClickFix/HTA; pairing those names with user-writable execution paths and a script/browser parent isolates trojanized copies from legitimate first-run installs. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/uat-11795-deploys-novel-starland-rat-and-bespoke-wldr-c2-implant-in-financially-motivated-campaign/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/russian-hackers-trojanize-webex-zoom-apps-to-push-starland-malware/
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1036.005 T1218.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Genuine Zoom/WebEx first-run installers staging in %Temp% before elevation
  • User double-clicking a legitimate DBeaver portable build from Downloads
  • IT-packaged MobaXterm deployment run from a staging folder
  • FaceIT anti-cheat updater writing to AppData
Suppression filter
| where ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName !in~ ("Mobatek","Cisco Systems, Inc.","Zoom Video Communications, Inc.","DBeaver Corp","DBeaver Corp.","FACEIT LTD") or isempty(ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName)
Response runbook
1) Triage: check the binary's signer/ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName against the real vendor and its SHA256 against VT; a mismatch or unsigned build is decisive. 2) Contain: quarantine the binary, isolate the host, and hunt the process tree for a following curl.exe→powershell.exe stager. 3) Hunt: sweep the org for the same SHA256 and for the download referrer/URL, and review the user's browser history/UrlClickEvents for the ClickFix lure page.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName matches regex @"(?i)(mobaxterm|webex|zoom|dbeaver|faceit).*\.exe$"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Downloads\", @"\AppData\Local\Temp\", @"\AppData\Roaming\", @"\Users\Public\")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("mshta.exe","chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","explorer.exe","powershell.exe","cmd.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName, SHA256, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName matches regex @"(?i)(mobaxterm|webex|zoom|dbeaver|faceit).*\.exe$"
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\\Downloads\\", "\\Temp\\", "\\Roaming\\", "\\Public\\")
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("mshta.exe","chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","explorer.exe","powershell.exe","cmd.exe")
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, ParentProcessName, CommandLine

pepesoft.exe game-cheat surveillance payload dropped from pepegit666 GitHub/Hugging Face infra AIDelivery High
Hunts the Socket-reported NuGet game-cheat campaign where a .NET DotnetTool downloader fetches the second-stage surveillance binary pepesoft.exe from GitHub Releases and Hugging Face paths under user 'pepegit666' (and pepesoft.ru). The payload name and download infrastructure are unique, high-fidelity strings. Rationale: Socket names the exact payload (pepesoft.exe), the publisher handle (pepegit666) hosting on GitHub Releases + Hugging Face, and the operator domain pepesoft.ru — all unique strings that produce near-zero false positives. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev/blog/11-malicious-nuget-tools-pose-as-game-cheats • https://gbhackers.com/11-malicious-nuget-game-cheat-packages/
ATT&CKT1105 T1608.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Malware researcher intentionally detonating the sample in a lab
  • Security team retro-hunting the IOC with the binary staged for analysis
  • A benign unrelated file coincidentally named pepesoft.exe (extremely unlikely given the distinct name)
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the writing process is a dotnet/DotnetTool downloader and capture FileOriginUrl to verify the pepegit666 GitHub/Hugging Face source. 2) Contain: quarantine pepesoft.exe, isolate the host, and block pepesoft.ru and the pepegit666 GitHub/Hugging Face URLs at the proxy. 3) Hunt: review the host for DoH to dns.google (the campaign's resolver-evasion), Telegram bot traffic (screenshot exfil), and any NuGet DotnetTool installs matching the cheat package names (Albion/GTA5RP/Lineage2 etc.).
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "pepesoft.exe" or FileOriginUrl has_any ("pepegit666","pepesoft.ru")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, FileOriginUrl, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName =~ "pepesoft.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256

SAM registry hive dump during rapid intrusion (Spirals ransomware) AIExploitation High
Hunts the Spirals ransomware credential-access step where operators dumped the Security Account Manager (SAM) hive within a three-hour interactive session before network-wide encryption. Targets reg.exe/esentutl hive extraction of SAM/SYSTEM/SECURITY. Rationale: Symantec's Spirals write-up states the actor "dumped the Security Account Manager (SAM) hive"; reg save of HKLM\SAM (plus SYSTEM/SECURITY needed to decrypt it) is rarely legitimate in user space and is a decisive pre-lateral-movement signal. Cross-checked against: • https://www.security.com/threat-intelligence/ransomware-spirals-extortion • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/new-spirals-ransomware-encrypts-victim-network-in-under-24-hours/
ATT&CKT1003.002 T1003.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sysadmin backing up a registry hive before a change
  • DFIR/forensic collection tooling exporting SAM/SYSTEM
  • Migration utilities exporting registry hives
  • esentutl used for legitimate ESE database repair (non-SAM)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("backup.exe","wbengine.exe","veeam.backup.shell.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the parent process and logon session — a hive dump from a web-server context (w3wp.exe) or an interactive attacker session is high-severity; a scheduled backup job is likely benign. 2) Contain: isolate the host, force-reset local accounts, and disable/rotate credentials for any account cached on it. 3) Hunt: on the same host look for EDR-uninstall activity, revsocks/Chisel/Cloudflare Tunnel covert channels, PsExec/WMI fan-out, and the ransom note C:\RECOVERY_SECTION.log — Spirals encrypted the network in under 24h.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (FileName =~ "reg.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "save" and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("hklm\\sam","hklm\\system","hklm\\security"))
   or (FileName =~ "esentutl.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("sam","\\config\\"))
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where (NewProcessName endswith "\\reg.exe" and CommandLine has "save" and CommandLine has_any ("hklm\\sam","hklm\\system","hklm\\security"))
   or (NewProcessName endswith "\\esentutl.exe" and CommandLine has_any ("sam","\\config\\"))
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
title: SAM/SYSTEM Registry Hive Dump via reg.exe or esentutl (Spirals Ransomware)
id: 7d3f2a08-9c6b-41e2-8a10-2b3c4d5e6f71
description: Detects extraction of the SAM/SYSTEM/SECURITY hives via reg save or esentutl, matching the Spirals ransomware credential-access step.

logsource:
  category: process_creation

detection:
  selection_reg:
    Image|endswith: '\reg.exe'
    CommandLine|contains|all:
      - 'save'
      - 'hklm\'
    CommandLine|contains:
      - 'sam'
      - 'system'
      - 'security'
  selection_esent:
    Image|endswith: '\esentutl.exe'
    CommandLine|contains: 'sam'
  condition: selection_reg or selection_esent
level: high
source:windows.security @EventID:4688 ((@Image:(*\\reg.exe OR *\\REG.EXE) AND @CommandLine:(*save*hklm\\sam* OR *save*HKLM\\SAM* OR *save*hklm\\system* OR *save*hklm\\security*)) OR (@Image:(*\\esentutl.exe OR *\\ESENTUTL.EXE) AND @CommandLine:*sam*))
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/(reg|esentutl)\.exe$/i
| regex("(?i)(save.*hklm\\\\(sam|system|security)|esentutl.*sam)", field=CommandLine)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, CommandLine, ParentBaseFileName], function=count())

| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where ((Processes.process_name="reg.exe" AND Processes.process="*save*" AND (Processes.process="*hklm\\sam*" OR Processes.process="*hklm\\system*" OR Processes.process="*hklm\\security*")) OR (Processes.process_name="esentutl.exe" AND Processes.process="*sam*")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)`
IIS worker (w3wp.exe) spawning shell/recon processes — ASP.NET web shell (Spirals ransomware) AIExploitation High
Hunts the Spirals initial-access vector: an ASP.NET web shell on an internet-facing IIS server, surfaced when w3wp.exe spawns cmd/powershell or recon LOLBins. This is the foothold that preceded SAM dumping, EDR removal, and PsExec deployment within hours. Rationale: Symantec attributes Spirals' initial access to an ASP.NET web shell on an internet-facing IIS server; w3wp.exe spawning interactive shells or recon LOLBins is the canonical, telemetry-observable manifestation of that web shell. Cross-checked against: • https://www.security.com/threat-intelligence/ransomware-spirals-extortion • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/new-spirals-ransomware-encrypts-victim-network-in-under-24-hours/
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1190 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate web app shelling out to net.exe/whoami for diagnostics
  • App-deployment scripts running under the IIS app-pool identity
  • Monitoring/health-check tooling invoking cmd from w3wp
  • Custom .NET apps that legitimately spawn PowerShell for admin tasks
Suppression filter
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("whoami","net user","net group","nltest","/domain","systeminfo") or FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the child command line and the IIS site/app-pool identity; recon commands (whoami/net/nltest) or a base64 PowerShell from w3wp is a strong web-shell indicator. 2) Contain: pull the server offline or isolate it, image the IIS webroot to find the dropped .aspx web shell, and reset app-pool/service credentials. 3) Hunt: given Spirals' <24h timeline, immediately hunt the same host and adjacent hosts for SAM hive dumps, EDR removal, revsocks/Chisel/Cloudflare Tunnel, PsExec/WMI, and the C:\RECOVERY_SECTION.log note.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "w3wp.exe"
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","whoami.exe","net.exe","net1.exe","systeminfo.exe","nltest.exe","reg.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\\w3wp.exe"
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\\cmd.exe","\\powershell.exe","\\pwsh.exe","\\whoami.exe","\\net.exe","\\net1.exe","\\systeminfo.exe","\\nltest.exe","\\reg.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
title: IIS Worker Process Spawning Shell/Recon (ASP.NET Web Shell - Spirals)

description: Detects w3wp.exe spawning cmd/powershell or recon LOLBins, indicating an ASP.NET web shell as used for initial access by the Spirals ransomware operators.

Spirals ransom note C:\RECOVERY_SECTION.log written to disk AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the Spirals ransomware impact stage by detecting creation of its ransom note file, C:\RECOVERY_SECTION.log, which threatens data publication within six days and points victims to a Tor negotiation portal. This is a single, unique, post-encryption IOC. Rationale: Symantec documents Spirals dropping its ransom note at C:\RECOVERY_SECTION.log with a six-day data-leak deadline and Tor portal; the exact filename is a unique, near-zero-FP impact IOC. Cross-checked against: • https://www.security.com/threat-intelligence/ransomware-spirals-extortion • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/new-spirals-ransomware-encrypts-victim-network-in-under-24-hours/
ATT&CKT1486 T1657
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Analyst restoring the note artifact into a sandbox for review
  • Threat-intel team seeding the filename as a canary/honeyfile
  • Backup restore of a previously infected system's files
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the writing process and look for concurrent mass file rename/encryption on the host (Spirals uses intermittent encryption on >5MB files). 2) Contain: isolate the host immediately and any peer that received PsExec/WMI pushes, and preserve the note + a sample encrypted file for keying analysis. 3) Hunt: enterprise-wide sweep for RECOVERY_SECTION.log and for the intrusion prelude — IIS web shell, SAM dump, EDR uninstall, revsocks/Chisel/Cloudflare Tunnel — to scope every host touched inside the <24h window.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "RECOVERY_SECTION.log"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessSHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName =~ "RECOVERY_SECTION.log"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc

| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false

            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

AuditLogs

| where Result =~ "success"
| extend AppName = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].displayName),
         AppId   = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].id),
         User    = tostring(parse_json(tostring(InitiatedBy)).user.userPrincipalName)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, User, AppName, AppId, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

n8n Token Exchange Flaw Could Let Attackers Log In as Users From Another Issuer

The Hacker News
2026-07-16 4 use cases 2 techniques 3 kill-chain phases detected

n8n, the workflow automation platform, handed out the wrong accounts at login. On Enterprise instances configured to trust more than one external token issuer, it matched an incoming JWT to a local user on the&nbsp;sub&nbsp;claim alone and ignored&nbsp;iss. A valid token from issuer A carrying a&nbsp;sub&nbsp;that belongs to someone under issuer B logged you in as them. Their password never

Vulnerable n8n version exposed to CVE-2026-59208 cross-issuer token-exchange auth bypass AIExploitation High
Surfaces managed hosts running n8n at a version affected by CVE-2026-59208 (below 2.27.4, or exactly 2.28.0) so exposure can be remediated. Hunts the specific fixed-version floors the advisory names rather than a generic 'outdated software' check. Rationale: Anchors on the exact fixed-version floors from the advisory (below 2.27.4, and the singular vulnerable 2.28.0) plus CVE-2026-59208, confirmed by the n8n GitHub advisory GHSA-mq3m-f8x3-579w — high-fidelity because the version predicate is deterministic, not heuristic. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/n8n-io/n8n/security/advisories/GHSA-mq3m-f8x3-579w • https://cve.threatint.eu/CVE/CVE-2026-59208 • https://docs.n8n.io/changelog/release-notes-2.x
ATT&CKT1190 T1556
Data sourcesVulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • n8n instance at a vulnerable version but with token exchange disabled (N8N_TOKEN_EXCHANGE_TRUSTED_KEYS unset) — per n8n's scope statement this is NOT actually affected
  • n8n at a vulnerable version configured with only a single trusted issuer — precondition of 2+ issuers not met, so not exploitable
  • Community/self-hosted n8n that TVM catalogs as generic Node.js and cannot version-attribute (coverage gap, not a true FP)
  • Dev/test or air-gapped n8n instances that are not internet-facing OEM deployments
  • A different product string-matching 'n8n' in the software inventory name
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the running n8n version and, critically, whether token exchange is actually on — check for N8N_TOKEN_EXCHANGE_TRUSTED_KEYS and whether 2+ external issuers are trusted; only then is the host truly exploitable. 2) Contain: upgrade to 2.28.1+ (or 2.27.4 on the 2.27 line); if patching must wait, cut the trusted-issuer list back to a single issuer or disable the token-exchange preview flag. 3) Hunt: review n8n auth/session logs for logins where the presenting token's iss does not match the target account's enrolled issuer, and check for CVE-2026-54305 Dynamic Credentials abuse on the same Enterprise surface.
DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where SoftwareName has "n8n"
| where (parse_version(SoftwareVersion) < parse_version("2.27.4")) or (SoftwareVersion == "2.28.0")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, DeviceId, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, EndOfSupportStatus
| order by DeviceName asc
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId == "CVE-2026-59208" or (SoftwareName has "n8n" and ((parse_version(SoftwareVersion) < parse_version("2.27.4")) or SoftwareVersion == "2.28.0"))
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, DeviceId, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel
| order by DeviceName asc

n8n token-exchange feature enabled — CVE-2026-59208 exploitation precondition (N8N_TOKEN_EXCHANGE_TRUSTED_KEYS) AIReconnaissance Medium
Surfaces hosts where n8n is launched with the token-exchange feature configured via the N8N_TOKEN_EXCHANGE_TRUSTED_KEYS environment variable, the exact precondition that makes CVE-2026-59208 reachable. Directly supports the advisory's 'work out what you are running' remediation step. Rationale: Anchors on the exact environment-variable string N8N_TOKEN_EXCHANGE_TRUSTED_KEYS named in the article as the token-exchange config; the flaw only reaches an instance when this feature is on, so process-command-line hits (e.g. `docker run -e N8N_TOKEN_EXCHANGE_TRUSTED_KEYS=...`) pinpoint exploitable hosts. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/n8n-io/n8n/security/advisories/GHSA-mq3m-f8x3-579w • https://docs.n8n.io/changelog/release-notes-2.x
ATT&CKT1190 T1556
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate OEM/embed deployment intentionally using token exchange with a single trusted issuer (enabled but not vulnerable)
  • Config passed via env-file, systemd unit, Kubernetes pod spec or compose secret rather than the CLI — visible as a benign hit or missed entirely (coverage gap)
  • Administrator inspecting/echoing the variable name during patch-verification or documentation work
  • CI/CD or IaC provisioning jobs that reference the variable while deploying n8n
  • Backup or config-audit scripts that grep for the variable name across hosts
Response runbook
1) Triage: on each hit confirm how many external issuers are trusted — a single issuer is safe, 2+ is the CVE-2026-59208 exploit condition; capture the running n8n version. 2) Contain: if 2+ issuers and version < 2.27.4 or == 2.28.0, upgrade to 2.28.1+, or immediately reduce to one trusted issuer / disable the preview flag. 3) Hunt: pull n8n session logs for the exposure window and look for authentications where a token's iss differs from the target user's enrolled issuer, and for the same sub value arriving from two issuers.

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Malicious wtsapi32.dll planted in ViPNet Update System directory (HelloNet delivery)
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Article-specific behavioural hunt — HelloNet campaign — new malicious modules launched through the ViPNet update sys
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] itcsrvup64.exe side-loads wtsapi32.dll from non-System32 path (HelloInjector execution) · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Renamed PuTTY reverse SSH tunnel to HelloNet C2 (frontpage.exe -R to 5.39.253.206) · [LLM] HelloProxy socket-logging artifact tesh4RPC.txt dropped in C:\Users\Public · [LLM] Outbound connection to HelloNet C2 5.39.253.206 (SSH tunnel / proxy egress) · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] HelloExecutor ViPNet key-export reconnaissance via svchost-spawned shell · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Malicious wtsapi32.dll planted in ViPNet Update System directory (HelloNet delivery) AIDelivery High
Hunts the HelloNet supply-chain delivery step: an attacker-supplied wtsapi32.dll dropped into C:\Program Files (x86)\InfoTeCS\VIPNet Update System so the startup binary itcsrvup64.exe side-loads it. wtsapi32.dll is a genuine Windows DLL that lives in System32 — its appearance inside the ViPNet update folder is the anomaly. Rationale: Anchors on the exact filename (wtsapi32.dll) and exact directory (InfoTeCS\VIPNet Update System) from the article; this DLL never legitimately resides there, so the write itself is high-fidelity. Corroborated by Positive Technologies' independent write-up of the same DLL-hijack path. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/tr/hellonet-vipnet/120700/ • https://www.securitylab.ru/news/574941.php • https://hijacklibs.net/entries/microsoft/built-in/wtsapi32.html
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1574.002 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • InfoTeCS/administrator staging a legitimate ViPNet update package that coincidentally bundles wtsapi32.dll (verify signature/hash)
  • Backup or EDR agent restoring the folder from a snapshot
  • Security team replaying the IOC in a sandbox on a monitored host
  • Manual copy of System32\wtsapi32.dll into the folder during troubleshooting
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessVersionInfoCompanyName has_any ("InfoTeCS","Microsoft") and InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("msiexec.exe","itcsrvup64.exe"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the SHA256 of the dropped wtsapi32.dll and compare against Microsoft's signed System32 copy; check digital signature — the genuine DLL is Microsoft-signed, the HelloInjector is not. Note the InitiatingProcess that wrote it. 2) Contain: isolate the host, quarantine the DLL, and suspend the ViPNet update service (itcsrvup64.exe) to stop side-load-on-boot. 3) Hunt: sweep every ViPNet host for wtsapi32.dll outside System32, then pivot to itcsrvup64.exe image-loads, svchost netsvcs injection, C2 to 5.39.253.206, and tesh4RPC.txt in C:\Users\Public.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "wtsapi32.dll"
| where FolderPath has @"\InfoTeCS\VIPNet Update System"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName =~ "wtsapi32.dll"
| where TargetFilePath has @"\InfoTeCS\VIPNet Update System"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

itcsrvup64.exe side-loads wtsapi32.dll from non-System32 path (HelloInjector execution) AIInstallation High
Detects execution of the side-load: the ViPNet startup binary itcsrvup64.exe loading wtsapi32.dll from its own program directory instead of the OS System32 copy. This is the moment HelloInjector runs prior to svchost.exe injection. Rationale: itcsrvup64.exe loading wtsapi32.dll from anywhere but System32/WinSxS is the exact side-load mechanism named in the article; the parent+DLL+path combination is not seen in benign operation. SPL/Sentinel left empty as CIM/ASIM have no image-load data model. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/tr/hellonet-vipnet/120700/ • https://www.securitylab.ru/news/574941.php
ATT&CKT1574.002 T1055.001
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate ViPNet build where InfoTeCS genuinely ships a wtsapi32.dll alongside itcsrvup64.exe (validate signer)
  • A repackaged/portable ViPNet install placing DLLs in a custom directory
  • DLL redirection via a .local manifest during vendor QA testing
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the loaded wtsapi32.dll path and hash; a System32 load is benign, a program-dir load is the side-load. Capture itcsrvup64.exe PID for the injection pivot. 2) Contain: isolate host, stop the ViPNet update service, quarantine the DLL. 3) Hunt: from the itcsrvup64.exe PID, look for svchost.exe (netsvcs) receiving injected code, listeners on ports 5003/5060, and outbound to 5.39.253.206.
DeviceImageLoadEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "itcsrvup64.exe"
| where FileName =~ "wtsapi32.dll"
| where FolderPath !startswith @"C:\Windows\System32" and FolderPath !startswith @"C:\Windows\WinSxS"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessId
| order by Timestamp desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
DeviceImageLoadEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "itcsrvup64.exe"
| where FileName =~ "wtsapi32.dll"
| where FolderPath !startswith @"C:\Windows\System32" and FolderPath !startswith @"C:\Windows\WinSxS"
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessId
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: itcsrvup64.exe Side-Loads wtsapi32.dll From ViPNet Program Directory
id: c2f4a5b3-9d8e-4c0f-b1a2-3d4e5f6a7b8c
description: Detects HelloInjector side-loading via itcsrvup64.exe loading wtsapi32.dll from a non-System32 path.
references:
  - https://securelist.com/tr/hellonet-vipnet/120700/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/16
tags:
  - attack.t1574.002
  - attack.t1055.001
logsource:
  category: image_load
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    Image|endswith: '\itcsrvup64.exe'
    ImageLoaded|endswith: '\wtsapi32.dll'
  filter_system32:
    ImageLoaded|startswith:
      - 'C:\Windows\System32'
      - 'C:\Windows\WinSxS'
  condition: selection and not filter_system32
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:7 @Image:(*\\itcsrvup64.exe OR *\\ITCSRVUP64.EXE) @ImageLoaded:(*\\wtsapi32.dll OR *\\WTSAPI32.DLL) -@ImageLoaded:(C\:\\Windows\\System32\\* OR C\:\\Windows\\WinSxS\\*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\\itcsrvup64\.exe$/i
| join({#event_simpleName=ClassifiedModuleLoad ImageFileName=/\\wtsapi32\.dll$/i NOT ImageFileName=/\\System32\\/i}, field=[aid], include=[ImageFileName])
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName], function=count())
Renamed PuTTY reverse SSH tunnel to HelloNet C2 (frontpage.exe -R to 5.39.253.206) AICommand & Control High
Detects the HelloNet operator pivot: a renamed PuTTY binary (frontpage.exe run from C:\Users\Public\Music) opening a reverse SSH tunnel (-R) to the C2 5.39.253.206 on port 3522, forwarding local 8443 to the internal HelloProxy port 5003. Both the masqueraded name/path and the reverse-tunnel-to-C2 command line are article-specific. Rationale: Uses the literal C2 IP 5.39.253.206, the reverse-tunnel flag -R, and the masqueraded binary/path (Public\Music\frontpage.exe = renamed PuTTY) straight from the article's command line; each alone is rare, together they are unambiguous. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/tr/hellonet-vipnet/120700/
ATT&CKT1572 T1090 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A sysadmin legitimately using PuTTY reverse tunnels for remote support (but not from Public\Music, not to 5.39.253.206)
  • Red-team/pentest replaying the exact PuTTY command during an engagement
  • A media app legitimately named frontpage.exe living in a Music folder (validate it is not a PuTTY binary via file description)
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm frontpage.exe file metadata shows PuTTY/plink internals and capture the full -R forwarding spec and the -pw credential used. 2) Contain: isolate host, kill the tunnel process, block 5.39.253.206:3522 at the firewall, and rotate any credential exposed in the -pw argument. 3) Hunt: enumerate other hosts running frontpage.exe or any -R tunnel to 5.39.253.206/5003, and correlate with HelloProxy listeners (5003/5060) and svchost injection.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (ProcessCommandLine has "5.39.253.206" and ProcessCommandLine has " -R ")
    or (FolderPath has @"\users\public\music\" and FileName =~ "frontpage.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where (ActingProcessCommandLine has "5.39.253.206" and ActingProcessCommandLine has " -R ")
    or (ActingProcessName has @"\users\public\music\" and ActingProcessName endswith "frontpage.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

HelloProxy socket-logging artifact tesh4RPC.txt dropped in C:\Users\Public AICommand & Control High
Detects creation of the HelloProxy operational log file C:\Users\Public\tesh4RPC.txt, which the in-svchost proxy writes for every AFD_RECV-triggered incoming message (threadid/pid entries). The exact filename in a world-writable directory is a clean article-specific IOC. Rationale: tesh4RPC.txt is a unique, non-dictionary filename named verbatim in the article as the HelloProxy AFD_RECV log; its write into C:\Users\Public — often by an unexpected svchost context — is near-zero-FP. The writing process (svchost) is surfaced for the injection pivot. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/tr/hellonet-vipnet/120700/
ATT&CKT1090 T1071.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Analyst copying the IOC file onto a monitored host for testing
  • Backup/restore tooling replaying a Public folder snapshot
  • A benign application coincidentally using the identical random-looking name (extremely unlikely)
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the process (ContextImageFileName/InitiatingProcessFileName) that wrote tesh4RPC.txt — expect svchost.exe; read the file for threadid/pid entries confirming proxy activity. 2) Contain: isolate host, capture memory of the writing svchost PID, quarantine the file. 3) Hunt: on the same host look for listeners on 5003/5060, the 0x0502 handshake / ASDFASFSAFASDF traffic, itcsrvup64.exe side-load, and the frontpage.exe tunnel to 5.39.253.206.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "tesh4RPC.txt"
| where FolderPath has @"\Users\Public"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessId, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName =~ "tesh4RPC.txt"
| where TargetFilePath has @"\Users\Public"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessId, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

HelloExecutor ViPNet key-export reconnaissance via svchost-spawned shell AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects the HelloExecutor recon fingerprint: a shell enumerating InfoTeCS/ViPNet directories — specifically the ViPNet Administrator key-container export path (kc\Export) and ViPNet Client\Export — where secure-network key material lives. High fidelity because it targets ViPNet's sensitive export folders, and the shell is typically spawned by an injected svchost.exe. Rationale: Anchored on the article's exact recon commands enumerating infotecs\ViPNet Administrator\kc\Export and ViPNet Client\Export — the directories holding ViPNet key/certificate material; benign users rarely `dir` these paths, and a svchost.exe parent confirms the injected-shell context. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/tr/hellonet-vipnet/120700/
ATT&CKT1083 T1059.003 T1552.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A ViPNet administrator legitimately auditing key-export folders
  • Backup software indexing the ViPNet Administrator directory
  • Helpdesk scripting an inventory of infotecs install paths during troubleshooting
  • EDR/vuln scanner enumerating installed software directories
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("explorer.exe","mmc.exe","powershell_ise.exe") or InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "svchost.exe"
Response runbook
1) Triage: check the parent of the shell — a services.exe→svchost.exe→cmd.exe chain with no interactive user strongly indicates HelloExecutor injection; review the full recon sequence (query user, ipconfig /all, net user/group). 2) Contain: isolate host, capture svchost memory, preserve any staged output. 3) Hunt: look for exfil of ViPNet key material, the frontpage.exe tunnel to 5.39.253.206, HelloCleaner log-wiping of ViPNet logs, and tesh4RPC.txt.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "infotecs"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any (@"\kc\Export", @"ViPNet Client\Export", @"ViPNet Administrator")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessId
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "infotecs"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any (@"\kc\Export", @"ViPNet Client\Export", @"ViPNet Administrator")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Outbound connection to HelloNet C2 5.39.253.206 (SSH tunnel / proxy egress) AICommand & Control Medium
Detects any host reaching the HelloNet command server 5.39.253.206, over which the operators run the reverse SSH tunnel (port 3522) forwarding to the internal HelloProxy port 5003. A direct-IP IOC match on confirmed campaign infrastructure. Rationale: Direct match on the campaign C2 IP 5.39.253.206 named in the article; the initiating process (frontpage.exe/renamed PuTTY or an injected svchost) and RemotePort 3522 are surfaced to distinguish tunnel vs proxy traffic. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/tr/hellonet-vipnet/120700/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1571 T1572
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel/sandbox detonation reaching the IOC from a research host
  • A security scanner probing the flagged IP for reachability
  • IP later re-provisioned by the hosting provider (5.39.253.x is a known bulletproof/VPS range) to a benign tenant — re-validate freshness
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process and port — frontpage.exe/plink to :3522 confirms the SSH tunnel; svchost.exe egress confirms proxy C2. 2) Contain: block 5.39.253.206 at the perimeter, isolate the host, terminate the connecting process. 3) Hunt: sweep all hosts for any contact with 5.39.253.206, then pivot to the wtsapi32.dll side-load, tesh4RPC.txt, and ViPNet key-export recon on those hosts.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "5.39.253.206"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Protocol, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstIpAddr == "5.39.253.206"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkApplicationProtocol, DstUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`

| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("16c211c96735f2fae9361b89bd7a31bf", "1bfe2b9493128574907a8279256a8bcc", "f9eed2f0158dc98e7012fb809152209c", "6001829a128fe264b4403138700c11a8", "ee4ff46ddd8489e81447962f927bc3f6", "41c938b3cd7e55d4077e34976929b140", "b103cd21280b4061f88b2bcc51394894", "9f5606a0755bc633b9bd7db6d179c09e", "0cfdffc56f0fa325d0c4d24780b46597") or SHA1 in~ ("16c211c96735f2fae9361b89bd7a31bf", "1bfe2b9493128574907a8279256a8bcc", "f9eed2f0158dc98e7012fb809152209c", "6001829a128fe264b4403138700c11a8", "ee4ff46ddd8489e81447962f927bc3f6", "41c938b3cd7e55d4077e34976929b140", "b103cd21280b4061f88b2bcc51394894", "9f5606a0755bc633b9bd7db6d179c09e", "0cfdffc56f0fa325d0c4d24780b46597") or MD5 in~ ("16c211c96735f2fae9361b89bd7a31bf", "1bfe2b9493128574907a8279256a8bcc", "f9eed2f0158dc98e7012fb809152209c", "6001829a128fe264b4403138700c11a8", "ee4ff46ddd8489e81447962f927bc3f6", "41c938b3cd7e55d4077e34976929b140", "b103cd21280b4061f88b2bcc51394894", "9f5606a0755bc633b9bd7db6d179c09e", "0cfdffc56f0fa325d0c4d24780b46597")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("16c211c96735f2fae9361b89bd7a31bf", "1bfe2b9493128574907a8279256a8bcc", "f9eed2f0158dc98e7012fb809152209c", "6001829a128fe264b4403138700c11a8", "ee4ff46ddd8489e81447962f927bc3f6", "41c938b3cd7e55d4077e34976929b140", "b103cd21280b4061f88b2bcc51394894", "9f5606a0755bc633b9bd7db6d179c09e", "0cfdffc56f0fa325d0c4d24780b46597") or SHA1 in~ ("16c211c96735f2fae9361b89bd7a31bf", "1bfe2b9493128574907a8279256a8bcc", "f9eed2f0158dc98e7012fb809152209c", "6001829a128fe264b4403138700c11a8", "ee4ff46ddd8489e81447962f927bc3f6", "41c938b3cd7e55d4077e34976929b140", "b103cd21280b4061f88b2bcc51394894", "9f5606a0755bc633b9bd7db6d179c09e", "0cfdffc56f0fa325d0c4d24780b46597") or MD5 in~ ("16c211c96735f2fae9361b89bd7a31bf", "1bfe2b9493128574907a8279256a8bcc", "f9eed2f0158dc98e7012fb809152209c", "6001829a128fe264b4403138700c11a8", "ee4ff46ddd8489e81447962f927bc3f6", "41c938b3cd7e55d4077e34976929b140", "b103cd21280b4061f88b2bcc51394894", "9f5606a0755bc633b9bd7db6d179c09e", "0cfdffc56f0fa325d0c4d24780b46597")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["16c211c96735f2fae9361b89bd7a31bf", "1bfe2b9493128574907a8279256a8bcc", "f9eed2f0158dc98e7012fb809152209c", "6001829a128fe264b4403138700c11a8", "ee4ff46ddd8489e81447962f927bc3f6", "41c938b3cd7e55d4077e34976929b140", "b103cd21280b4061f88b2bcc51394894", "9f5606a0755bc633b9bd7db6d179c09e", "0cfdffc56f0fa325d0c4d24780b46597"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

GoSerpent ThumbcacheService staging DB (thumbcache_605a.db) written to C:\Users\Public AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts creation of the ThumbcacheService collection database thumbcache_605a.db in C:\Users\Public\, where GoSerpent stages harvested .doc/.docx/.pdf/.xls/.xlsx documents before exfiltration. Legitimate Windows thumbnail caches use the same thumbcache_*.db naming but live under AppData\Local\Microsoft\Windows\Explorer, never in the Public profile, making the Public-path variant article-specific. Rationale: Anchored on the article's verbatim filename thumbcache_605a.db (code block) and the C:\Users\Public\ staging path; legitimate thumbcache DBs never live in the Public profile, so the path variant catches renamed samples with near-zero FP. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/goserpent-backdoor-in-southeast-asia/120687/
ATT&CKT1074.001 T1119
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A user or admin manually copying their AppData thumbnail cache into C:\Users\Public for troubleshooting
  • Backup/migration tooling that mirrors user profile Explorer caches into a shared Public folder
  • Forensic/IR tools exporting thumbcache artifacts to C:\Users\Public for analysis
  • A security researcher detonating the sample in a lab on a monitored host
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has @"\Windows\explorer.exe"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify InitiatingProcessFileName that wrote the DB; a service DLL host (svchost.exe hosting an unknown service) or a binary in Public/Temp is high-suspicion. Inspect the file for a 7-Zip archive nearby and confirm it is not a genuine Explorer cache. 2) Contain: isolate the host, capture the DB and any adjacent .7z archives for analysis, and disable/stop the suspicious Windows service backing ThumbcacheService. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same host for 7-Zip archiving with the campaign password, lass.exe/updates.exe processes, and SAM/LSASS credential-dumping activity in the prior days.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "thumbcache_605a.db"
    or (FolderPath has @"\Users\Public\" and FileName startswith "thumbcache_" and FileName endswith ".db")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName =~ "thumbcache_605a.db"
    or (TargetFilePath has @"\Users\Public\" and TargetFileName startswith "thumbcache_" and TargetFileName endswith ".db")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

GoSerpent 7-Zip archiving with hardcoded campaign password @vx0a9n5W2M0c3D6.# AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts ThumbcacheService's 7-Zip archiving stage, which packs collected documents into password-protected archives using the fixed password @vx0a9n5W2M0c3D6.# with a 20MB volume limit. The password string is a unique campaign artifact, so any command line containing it is effectively a signature regardless of the archiver binary name. Rationale: The password @vx0a9n5W2M0c3D6.# is a verbatim campaign string with effectively zero legitimate use; matching its alphanumeric core (vx0a9n5W2M0c3D6) survives quoting/escaping and catches renamed 7z binaries. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/goserpent-backdoor-in-southeast-asia/120687/
ATT&CKT1560.001 T1074.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Analyst re-running the sample's archive command during malware analysis on a lab host
  • Threat-intel/IR playbook that references the password string in a script comment for testing detections
  • Purple-team exercise emulating GoSerpent's archiving stage
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the archiver binary (7z.exe/7za.exe or a renamed copy) and the target file set; look for the -v20m volume flag and the source documents being packed. 2) Contain: isolate the host, preserve the produced archives, and block outbound to any network share the archives were destined for. 3) Hunt: locate thumbcache_605a.db on the same host, review the credential-dumping activity that supplied the share credentials, and check network-share write events for exfiltration of the archives.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "vx0a9n5W2M0c3D6"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where CommandLine has "vx0a9n5W2M0c3D6"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

GoSerpent/McMx masquerading proxy binaries lass.exe and updates.exe AIInstallation High
Hunts execution of GoSerpent's masquerading binaries lass.exe (mimicking lsass.exe) and updates.exe, which host the SOCKS5 proxy/RAT. lass.exe is never a legitimate Windows binary, and updates.exe running from user-writable/staging directories is a strong anomaly for this campaign. Rationale: lass.exe and updates.exe are named verbatim in the article (code blocks) as GoSerpent's process-masquerading filenames; lass.exe has no legitimate counterpart and the path constraint on updates.exe filters the common legitimate updater binaries. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/goserpent-backdoor-in-southeast-asia/120687/
ATT&CKT1036.005 T1090.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate third-party application shipping its own updates.exe from ProgramData/AppData (e.g. some auto-updaters)
  • Developer/test binary coincidentally named lass.exe in a source tree
  • Software packaging or installer temp extraction dropping an updates.exe into a Temp directory
  • Portable app launched from a USB/Public share named updates.exe
Suppression filter
| where not (FileName =~ "updates.exe" and InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("msiexec.exe","setup.exe"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the SHA256 and signer of the process; unsigned lass.exe or a Go-compiled updates.exe from a user-writable path is high-confidence. Check for a listening socket / SOCKS5 behavior and outbound C2 from the same PID. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the process, and block the associated C2 IPs at the perimeter. 3) Hunt: search for ThumbcacheService staging (thumbcache_605a.db), the 7-Zip archive password, and credential-dumping tools deployed by the same backdoor across the environment.

GoSerpent QuarksDumpLocalHash / SAM hive local hash extraction AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the QuarksDumpLocalHash tool GoSerpent deploys to extract local account password hashes from the SAM registry hive for offline cracking, plus the equivalent reg.exe SAM/SECURITY hive save. This is distinct from LSASS memory access and targets the on-disk SAM credential store. Rationale: Anchored on the named tool QuarksDumpLocalHash and its documented SAM-hive extraction behavior; the reg.exe hive-save branch catches the same TTP if the operator uses a LOLBin instead of the custom tool, and it deliberately avoids overlapping the existing LSASS-access detection. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/goserpent-backdoor-in-southeast-asia/120687/
ATT&CKT1003.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sysadmin exporting a SAM/SECURITY hive for legitimate password-audit or migration tooling
  • Endpoint hardening/audit software (e.g. compliance scanners) reading local hive backups
  • IR/forensics collection scripts that reg save HKLM\SAM for evidence
  • Backup software snapshotting registry hives
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("forensic_collector.exe","psexec.exe") and not (InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "cmd.exe" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "backup")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the parent process and account; a hive save or quarks* binary spawned by an unknown Go backdoor (lass.exe/updates.exe) rather than an admin session is high-confidence. Check whether the resulting hive/hash output was written to a staging path. 2) Contain: isolate the host, force-reset local account passwords (and any domain accounts used interactively), and revoke cached credentials. 3) Hunt: correlate with ThumbcacheService staging and network-share writes — the dumped credentials are used to authenticate to shares for exfiltration; review share-access logs for the affected accounts.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName has "quarks" or ProcessCommandLine has "QuarksDumpLocalHash"
    or (FileName =~ "reg.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "save" and ProcessCommandLine has_any (@"hklm\sam", @"hklm\security"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has "quarks" or CommandLine has "QuarksDumpLocalHash"
    or (NewProcessName endswith @"\reg.exe" and CommandLine has "save" and (CommandLine has @"hklm\sam" or CommandLine has @"hklm\security"))
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: GoSerpent QuarksDumpLocalHash SAM Hive Dump
id: d70e2b19-3c84-4a56-b0f1-9a2c4e7d6b12
description: Detects QuarksDumpLocalHash or reg.exe saving the SAM/SECURITY hive to extract local password hashes, as deployed by the GoSerpent backdoor.
references:
  - https://securelist.com/goserpent-backdoor-in-southeast-asia/120687/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/16
tags:
  - attack.credential_access
  - attack.t1003.002
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_tool:
    CommandLine|contains: 'QuarksDumpLocalHash'
  selection_toolname:
    Image|contains: 'quarks'
  selection_regsave:
    Image|endswith: '\reg.exe'
    CommandLine|contains: 'save'
    CommandLine|contains:
      - 'hklm\sam'
      - 'hklm\security'
  condition: selection_tool or selection_toolname or selection_regsave
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 (@Image:(*\QuarksDumpLocalHash.exe OR *\quarksdumplocalhash.exe) OR @CommandLine:(*QuarksDumpLocalHash* OR *quarksdumplocalhash*) OR (@Image:(*\reg.exe OR *\REG.EXE) AND @CommandLine:(*save* OR *SAVE*) AND @CommandLine:(*HKLM\SAM* OR *hklm\sam* OR *HKLM\SECURITY* OR *hklm\security*)))
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| ImageFileName=/quarks/i OR CommandLine=/QuarksDumpLocalHash/i OR (ImageFileName=/\\reg\.exe$/i AND CommandLine=/save/i AND CommandLine=/hklm\\(sam|security)/i)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ImageFileName, CommandLine, ParentBaseFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name="*quarks*" OR Processes.process="*QuarksDumpLocalHash*" OR (Processes.process_name="reg.exe" AND Processes.process="*save*" AND (Processes.process="*hklm\\sam*" OR Processes.process="*hklm\\security*"))) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name="*quarks*" OR Processes.process="*QuarksDumpLocalHash*" OR (Processes.process_name="reg.exe" AND Processes.process="*save*" AND (Processes.process="*hklm\\sam*" OR Processes.process="*hklm\\security*"))) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] PhantomEnigma police-themed phishing via compromised .gov.br mailboxes and lookalike domains · [LLM] PhantomEnigma delivery-host callout to compromised/lookalike .gov.br installers · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] PhantomEnigma patched Electron/Boostnote index.js backdoor Run-key persistence · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] PhantomEnigma backdoor ~180-second C2 beacon from Electron/Node process · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains

PhantomEnigma police-themed phishing via compromised .gov.br mailboxes and lookalike domains AIDelivery Medium
Hunts inbound emails carrying PhantomEnigma's Brazilian police lures ('Ofício Polícia Civil', 'Procuração Digital') or links to the campaign's compromised/lookalike .gov.br delivery hosts. Because the mails are sent from compromised mailboxes and pass SPF/DKIM/DMARC, this pivots on lure content and destination host rather than auth failure. Rationale: Uses the article's exact Portuguese lure titles ('Ofício Polícia Civil'/'Procuração Digital') and the named compromised/lookalike .gov.br hosts as URL-domain IOCs; auth-pass mails from compromised mailboxes defeat SPF/DKIM checks, so content+destination pivots are the only reliable signal. Sentinel left empty: this tenant's provided Sentinel schema has no EmailEvents/message-tracking equivalent. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/20-hijacked-government-websites.html • https://any.run/cybersecurity-blog/phantomenigma-malware-analysis/

Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full message via NetworkMessageId — inspect SenderMailFromDomain vs SenderFromDomain, the AuthenticationDetails, and whether the URL redirects to an installer (Inno/MSI). 2) Contain: soft-delete/quarantine matching mails tenant-wide (EmailPostDelivery), block the delivery host at the proxy, reset any internal mailbox seen sending these. 3) Hunt: for every recipient who clicked, pivot to DeviceProcessEvents/DeviceNetworkEvents for Boostnote/node.exe execution and ~180s beacons (see companion UCs).
