PhantomEnigma delivery-host callout to compromised/lookalike .gov.br installers AIDelivery High
Detects endpoints resolving or connecting to the specific compromised municipal, public-security and judicial .gov.br hosts (and police-themed lookalikes) PhantomEnigma abuses as trusted redirect/installer staging. These legitimate-looking portals are the delivery infrastructure that fetches the Inno/MSI installer. Rationale: Keys on the exact compromised/lookalike .gov.br hostnames named in the article as delivery infrastructure — these are specific FQDNs, so a match is high-fidelity. IPs from the IOC set were deliberately dropped: several fall in Microsoft/Azure/Akamai ranges (40.126.31.128, 204.79.197.203, 88.221.169.205) and would generate FPs as standalone indicators. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/20-hijacked-government-websites.html • https://any.run/cybersecurity-blog/phantomenigma-malware-analysis/

PhantomEnigma patched Electron/Boostnote index.js backdoor Run-key persistence AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the backdoor's persistence step — a HKCU ...\CurrentVersion\Run value written to autostart the patched Electron host (Boostnote) whose app.asar index.js was replaced with the modular backdoor. Boostnote is a discontinued niche note app; its autostart entry in an enterprise is itself suspicious. Rationale: Uses the article's named host app (patched Boostnote) and the malicious index.js payload plus the login-settings persistence behavior; Electron's setLoginItemSettings writes exactly this HKCU Run value, so the (Run key + Boostnote/index.js) pair is a tight article-specific signal. Boostnote is EOL, lowering baseline noise. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/20-hijacked-government-websites.html • https://any.run/cybersecurity-blog/phantomenigma-malware-analysis/
ATT&CKT1547.001 T1554
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer who legitimately installed the discontinued Boostnote note app and enabled launch-on-login
  • Unrelated Electron apps whose Run value literally contains 'index.js' in a debug/dev launch string
  • Software-packaging/SCCM test images that register Boostnote autostart
  • Portable-app launchers that autostart from AppData
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("ccmexec.exe","msiexec.exe") and DeviceName has "BUILD")
Response runbook
1) Triage: read RegistryValueData for the full launch path — confirm it points into %AppData%/%LocalAppData% and which app.asar/index.js it invokes; check the writing process (InitiatingProcessFileName = installer or electron). 2) Contain: remove the Run value, quarantine the Boostnote install directory, isolate host. 3) Hunt: extract and review the patched index.js for eval()/beacon logic, then pivot to the ~180s C2 beacon UC and the machine-ID/campaign-tag file dropped beside the installer.
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("RegistryValueSet","RegistryKeyCreated")
| where RegistryKey has @"\CurrentVersion\Run"
| where RegistryValueData has "Boostnote" or (RegistryValueData has @"\AppData\" and RegistryValueData has "index.js")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImRegistryEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where RegistryKey has @"\CurrentVersion\Run"
| where RegistryValueData has "Boostnote" or (RegistryValueData has @"\AppData\" and RegistryValueData has "index.js")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, RegistryKey, RegistryValue, RegistryValueData, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

PhantomEnigma backdoor ~180-second C2 beacon from Electron/Node process AICommand & Control Medium
Detects the modular backdoor's command-poll behavior — a patched Electron/Node process beaconing to public infrastructure on a regular ~180-second cadence ('check for new commands every 180 seconds'). Targets node.exe / electron.exe / Boostnote.exe making sustained, evenly-spaced outbound connections a note-taking app has no reason to make. Rationale: Encodes the article's concrete 180-second command-poll cadence (>=8 distinct 3-minute bins ≈ regular beaconing) combined with the named patched-Electron host processes (Boostnote/Node.js); a note app beaconing on a fixed interval to public IPs is high-signal. Rotating C2 defeats static IP blocklists, so this pivots on process+periodicity, not a fixed destination. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/20-hijacked-government-websites.html • https://any.run/cybersecurity-blog/phantomenigma-malware-analysis/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1573
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legit Electron app doing genuine 3-minute update/telemetry polling
  • node.exe running a local dev server or CI agent polling an external API on a schedule
  • Boostnote's own (legacy) cloud-sync heartbeat if the real app is in use
  • Corporate software with fixed-interval license/heartbeat check-ins
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFolderPath has @"\Program Files\" and RemoteIP has_prefix "20.")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the process image path (AppData vs Program Files) and pull the destination — resolve WHOIS/ASN and check against the compromised .gov.br host list and known-good update endpoints. 2) Contain: isolate the endpoint, block the C2 IP/domain, capture the process memory and the patched index.js. 3) Hunt: decode the beacon format, look for eval()-driven second-stage downloads (DeviceFileEvents .exe drops), and sweep for the same process→interval pattern org-wide since C2 rotates.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(24h)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","electron.exe","Boostnote.exe")
| summarize ConnCount = count(), BeaconWindows = dcount(bin(Timestamp, 3m)), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where ConnCount >= 10 and BeaconWindows >= 8   // ~180s cadence sustained over >=24 min
| order by ConnCount desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where NetworkDirection == "Outbound" or isempty(NetworkDirection)
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(), BeaconWindows = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 3m)), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount >= 10 and BeaconWindows >= 8   // ~180s cadence sustained over >=24 min
| order by ConnCount desc
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:3 @Image:(*\\node.exe OR *\\Node.exe OR *\\electron.exe OR *\\Electron.exe OR *\\Boostnote.exe OR *\\boostnote.exe) NOT (CIDR(@DestinationIp, 10.0.0.0/8) OR CIDR(@DestinationIp, 172.16.0.0/12) OR CIDR(@DestinationIp, 192.168.0.0/16))
#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4 ContextImageFileName=/(node|electron|boostnote)\.exe$/i
| NOT cidr("10.0.0.0/8", field=RemoteAddressIP4)
| NOT cidr("172.16.0.0/12", field=RemoteAddressIP4)
| NOT cidr("192.168.0.0/16", field=RemoteAddressIP4)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, RemoteAddressIP4, RemotePort], function=count())
| _count > 10

| tstats summariesonly=false count as conn_count dc(_time) as distinct_secs min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where (All_Traffic.app="node.exe" OR All_Traffic.process="*node.exe" OR All_Traffic.process="*electron.exe" OR All_Traffic.process="*Boostnote.exe") All_Traffic.dest_is_internal=false by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.process All_Traffic.dest All_Traffic.dest_port span=3m | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | stats count as beacon_windows sum(conn_count) as total_conns min(firstTime) as firstTime max(lastTime) as lastTime by src process dest dest_port | where beacon_windows >= 8 AND total_conns >= 10 | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d06
status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1204.002
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\explorer.exe'
            - '\RuntimeBroker.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'

Stupig keyboard-layout DLL (kbdus1.dll/a.dll) loaded into winlogon.exe AIInstallation High
Hunts the Stupig pre-login backdoor loading its trojanized keyboard-layout DLL into winlogon.exe at boot. The module masquerades as the legitimate US-English layout kbdus.dll but is named kbdus1.dll (or a.dll), giving an operator SYSTEM command execution from the logon screen before any sign-in. Rationale: Uses the article's exact masquerade filenames (kbdus1.dll/a.dll vs legit kbdus.dll) plus the winlogon.exe load context and the Symantec-confirmed SHA256 5bb5cff... winlogon loading any keyboard DLL other than kbdus.dll is inherently anomalous. Cross-checked against Symantec/security.com which confirmed the DLL names and hash. Cross-checked against: • https://www.security.com/threat-intelligence/daxin-returns-stupig • https://cybersecuritynews.com/hackers-can-type-a-secret-username-at-the-windows-login-screen/
ATT&CKT1547.004 T1036.005
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Third-party IME/keyboard-layout software installing a non-Microsoft layout DLL under an unusual name
  • Legitimate multilingual layout DLLs (kbdusx.dll, kbdusl.dll) if the analyst broadens the name match
  • In-house accessibility tooling that hooks the logon desktop
  • Security product that injects a helper module into winlogon.exe
Suppression filter
| where not (SHA256 in~ ("") ) // retain hash TP; to suppress known-good OEM IME add: and InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "winlogon.exe"
Response runbook
1. Triage: confirm the loaded module path/hash; compare SHA256 against 5bb5cff... and verify the DLL is NOT the signed Microsoft kbdus.dll (check signer + FolderPath). 2. Contain: isolate the host — the DLL grants pre-auth SYSTEM shell; do not simply reboot (persistence reloads at startup). Capture memory before power actions. 3. Hunt: on the same host look for srt64.sys (Daxin driver), the Keyboard Layouts registry registration, and winlogon.exe spawning cmd/powershell; sweep the fleet for the same DLL name/hash.
DeviceImageLoadEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "winlogon.exe"
| where FileName in~ ("kbdus1.dll","a.dll")
    or SHA256 == "5bb5cffda4647940919a185df37aab2aef71ca3010a6c1d05bdcc8bc8fb3af3f"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessId, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.

DeviceImageLoadEvents

| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessId, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256

title: Stupig Trojanized Keyboard-Layout DLL Loaded by winlogon.exe
id: 6f2a1c84-7b03-4e9a-9d21-4c7e8b6a1f30
description: Detects winlogon.exe loading a keyboard-layout DLL masquerading as kbdus.dll (Stupig backdoor named kbdus1.dll or a.dll)
references:
  - https://www.security.com/threat-intelligence/daxin-returns-stupig
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/daxin-resurfaces-in-taiwan-alongside.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/16
tags:
  - attack.t1547.004
  - attack.t1036.005
logsource:
  category: image_load
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    Image|endswith: '\winlogon.exe'
    ImageLoaded|endswith:
      - '\kbdus1.dll'
      - '\a.dll'
  condition: selection
level: high
Malicious keyboard-layout registration pointing to Stupig DLL AIInstallation High
Detects Stupig establishing persistence by registering itself as a keyboard-layout provider so win32k.sys loads it into winlogon.exe. Fires when the 'Layout File' value under the Keyboard Layouts registry key is set to the malicious kbdus1.dll or a.dll instead of a legitimate Microsoft layout binary. Rationale: Anchors on the article's persistence mechanism (keyboard-layout provider registration causing win32k.sys to load the DLL into winlogon.exe) with the concrete malicious value data kbdus1.dll/a.dll. Legit layouts never point 'Layout File' at these names. Symantec/security.com corroborated the registration path and filenames. Cross-checked against: • https://www.security.com/threat-intelligence/daxin-returns-stupig • https://gbhackers.com/stupig-system-level-malware/
ATT&CKT1547.004 T1112
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Custom or OEM keyboard-layout packages that ship a vendor DLL and register a Layout File value
  • Enterprise imaging/GPO that provisions additional input languages at first boot
  • A benign in-house DLL that happens to be named a.dll referenced by a layout entry
  • Localization testing labs installing many non-standard layouts
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("tiptsf.dll","input.dll") and RegistryValueData !has "kbdus.dll"
Response runbook
1. Triage: pull the full RegistryKey (the layout ID subkey) and the initiating process — legitimate registration is done by system installers, not user processes; validate the referenced DLL's signer/hash. 2. Contain: isolate host, back up the registry hive, and remove the malicious layout entry only after forensic capture (loaded module stays resident in winlogon until reboot). 3. Hunt: correlate to the winlogon.exe DLL load (UC1), the srt64.sys driver, and any winlogon-spawned shells; sweep fleet registries for Layout File values referencing kbdus1.dll/a.dll.
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RegistryKey has @"\Control\Keyboard Layouts\"
| where RegistryValueName =~ "Layout File"
| where RegistryValueData has_any ("kbdus1.dll","a.dll")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImRegistryEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where RegistryKey has @"\Control\Keyboard Layouts\"
| where RegistryValue =~ "Layout File"
| where RegistryValueData has_any ("kbdus1.dll","a.dll")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, RegistryKey, RegistryValue, RegistryValueData, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
winlogon.exe spawning a command shell (Stupig pre-login SYSTEM execution) AIExploitation High
Detects the Stupig backdoor's payoff behaviour: after a 'stupig'-prefixed username is entered at the logon screen, the DLL running inside winlogon.exe spawns cmd.exe/PowerShell (or runs a command) as SYSTEM on the secure desktop. winlogon.exe is not a normal parent for interactive shells or recon tools. Rationale: Directly targets the article's described payoff — Stupig inside winlogon.exe spawning a SYSTEM cmd on the logon screen. winlogon's only legitimate children are userinit.exe/LogonUI.exe/fontdrvhost/dwm, so a shell or recon binary child is a high-fidelity SYSTEM-escalation signal independent of hashes. Behaviour confirmed across security.com and cybersecuritynews. Cross-checked against: • https://www.security.com/threat-intelligence/daxin-returns-stupig • https://cybersecuritynews.com/hackers-can-type-a-secret-username-at-the-windows-login-screen/
ATT&CKT1547.004 T1059.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Endpoint security/EDR validation tooling that intentionally spawns processes from winlogon during red-team tests
  • Legacy accessibility utilities or third-party credential providers launching helpers on the secure desktop
  • Some remote-assistance products injecting a shell into the logon session
  • Broken driver/OEM software mis-parenting a process to winlogon
Suppression filter
| where not (FileName =~ "cmd.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("\\Windows\\System32\\oobe\\","BdeUISrv"))
Response runbook
1. Triage: capture the child ProcessCommandLine and integrity level (expect SYSTEM) — a command line following the shell often reveals the operator's action; check who was physically/RDP at console. 2. Contain: isolate host and capture volatile memory before reboot (Stupig persists via the layout DLL). 3. Hunt: pivot to the kbdus1.dll/a.dll load and layout registration on the same host, look for srt64.sys, and review downstream child processes (net/whoami/reg) for lateral-movement recon.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "winlogon.exe"
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","net.exe","net1.exe","whoami.exe","cscript.exe","wscript.exe","reg.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessIntegrityLevel, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\\winlogon.exe"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\cmd.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\powershell.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\pwsh.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\net.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\net1.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\whoami.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\cscript.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\wscript.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\reg.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, TokenElevationType, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Daxin kernel rootkit driver srt64.sys drop / service install AIInstallation High
Detects installation of the Daxin kernel-mode rootkit as srt64.sys under System32\drivers, matched by name/path and the Symantec-confirmed SHA256. Daxin registers as a signed kernel driver, hijacks existing TCP connections for covert C2, and can reach air-gapped segments via multi-hop. Rationale: Uses the article's exact driver name/path (%SystemRoot%\System32\drivers\srt64.sys) and the Symantec-verified SHA256 49c827... The 7045 angle catches the kernel-driver service registration Daxin requires. Corroborated by security.com's 2026 report and the original 2022 Symantec Daxin analysis. Cross-checked against: • https://www.security.com/threat-intelligence/daxin-returns-stupig • https://symantec-enterprise-blogs.security.com/blogs/threat-intelligence/daxin-backdoor-espionage
ATT&CKT1014 T1543.003 T1205
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Unrelated legitimate drivers with similar short names (e.g. Symantec srtsp64.sys) if the analyst loosens the name match — the exact 'srt64.sys' + drivers path is specific
  • Backup/EDR agents installing kernel drivers during a maintenance window (distinguishable by signer and expected name)
  • Driver-signing test/QA machines loading many unsigned/renamed .sys files
  • Forensic/IR tooling dropping a driver by copy into drivers\ during response
Suppression filter
| where FileName =~ "srt64.sys" and FolderPath has @"\System32\drivers\" and InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("ccsvchst.exe","smc.exe")
Response runbook
1. Triage: confirm the file hash against 49c827... and inspect the driver's Authenticode signer/timestamp (Daxin carries a 2013 compile stamp) and the creating process. 2. Contain: isolate host from all network segments — Daxin hijacks existing TCP sessions and supports multi-hop to air-gapped hosts, so conventional egress blocking is insufficient; capture memory, then plan an offline reimage. 3. Hunt: check for Stupig co-infection (kbdus1.dll/a.dll, Keyboard Layouts registration, winlogon shell), review the host's TCP peers for downstream multi-hop victims, and sweep the fleet for the srt64.sys name/hash and matching 2013 compile timestamps.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(90d)
| where (FileName =~ "srt64.sys" and FolderPath has @"\System32\drivers\")
    or SHA256 == "49c827cf48efb122a9d6fd87b426482b7496ccd4a2dbca31ebbf6b2b80c98530"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(90d)
| where EventID == 7045
| where ServiceFileName has "srt64.sys"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, AccountName, ServiceName, ServiceFileName, ServiceType, ServiceStartType
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`

     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("49c827cf48efb122a9d6fd87b426482b7496ccd4a2dbca31ebbf6b2b80c98530", "5bb5cffda4647940919a185df37aab2aef71ca3010a6c1d05bdcc8bc8fb3af3f", "90b7b2c6f3d05234dc55678243039d7e51f0d54190239e5234a0005533337dc8", "643de2a1cf9148b896efecf560c9476fa56118ec477c4e15eb5c2da4b318061f") or SHA1 in~ ("49c827cf48efb122a9d6fd87b426482b7496ccd4a2dbca31ebbf6b2b80c98530", "5bb5cffda4647940919a185df37aab2aef71ca3010a6c1d05bdcc8bc8fb3af3f", "90b7b2c6f3d05234dc55678243039d7e51f0d54190239e5234a0005533337dc8", "643de2a1cf9148b896efecf560c9476fa56118ec477c4e15eb5c2da4b318061f") or MD5 in~ ("49c827cf48efb122a9d6fd87b426482b7496ccd4a2dbca31ebbf6b2b80c98530", "5bb5cffda4647940919a185df37aab2aef71ca3010a6c1d05bdcc8bc8fb3af3f", "90b7b2c6f3d05234dc55678243039d7e51f0d54190239e5234a0005533337dc8", "643de2a1cf9148b896efecf560c9476fa56118ec477c4e15eb5c2da4b318061f")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("49c827cf48efb122a9d6fd87b426482b7496ccd4a2dbca31ebbf6b2b80c98530", "5bb5cffda4647940919a185df37aab2aef71ca3010a6c1d05bdcc8bc8fb3af3f", "90b7b2c6f3d05234dc55678243039d7e51f0d54190239e5234a0005533337dc8", "643de2a1cf9148b896efecf560c9476fa56118ec477c4e15eb5c2da4b318061f") or SHA1 in~ ("49c827cf48efb122a9d6fd87b426482b7496ccd4a2dbca31ebbf6b2b80c98530", "5bb5cffda4647940919a185df37aab2aef71ca3010a6c1d05bdcc8bc8fb3af3f", "90b7b2c6f3d05234dc55678243039d7e51f0d54190239e5234a0005533337dc8", "643de2a1cf9148b896efecf560c9476fa56118ec477c4e15eb5c2da4b318061f") or MD5 in~ ("49c827cf48efb122a9d6fd87b426482b7496ccd4a2dbca31ebbf6b2b80c98530", "5bb5cffda4647940919a185df37aab2aef71ca3010a6c1d05bdcc8bc8fb3af3f", "90b7b2c6f3d05234dc55678243039d7e51f0d54190239e5234a0005533337dc8", "643de2a1cf9148b896efecf560c9476fa56118ec477c4e15eb5c2da4b318061f")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["49c827cf48efb122a9d6fd87b426482b7496ccd4a2dbca31ebbf6b2b80c98530", "5bb5cffda4647940919a185df37aab2aef71ca3010a6c1d05bdcc8bc8fb3af3f", "90b7b2c6f3d05234dc55678243039d7e51f0d54190239e5234a0005533337dc8", "643de2a1cf9148b896efecf560c9476fa56118ec477c4e15eb5c2da4b318061f"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Oracle EBS unauthenticated exploit POST to /OA_HTML/ibytransmit (CVE-2026-46817) AIExploitation High
Hunts inbound unauthenticated HTTP POST requests to the Oracle E-Business Suite Payments File Transmission endpoint /OA_HTML/ibytransmit, the exact code path abused by CVE-2026-46817 for arbitrary file read and Oracle Payments takeover. Legitimate iPayment file transmission is authenticated and internal, so external POSTs to this endpoint are the exploit itself. Rationale: Endpoint /OA_HTML/ibytransmit, POST method, and unauthenticated access are the confirmed exploit primitives for CVE-2026-46817 (cross-checked against Mallory and SoCRadar write-ups describing the ibytransmit + CODEX_PULL + FULL_FILE_PATH=/etc/passwd payload). Any external POST to this path is inherently anomalous. Cross-checked against: • https://www.mallory.ai/vulnerabilities/CVE-2026-46817 • https://socradar.io/blog/cve-2026-46817-oracle-payments-takeover/ • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/06/30/oracle-payments-cve-2026-46817-exploitation/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/oracle-e-business-suite-flaw-cve-2026.html
ATT&CKT1190 T1083
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authenticated vulnerability scanners (Tenable/Qualls/Rapid7) probing EBS for CVE-2026-46817
  • Oracle-authorized internal iPayment/CODEX file transmission jobs traversing a reverse proxy that rewrites source to external
  • Red-team / penetration-test validation of the patch
  • Shadowserver or other benign internet-wide scanners hitting the endpoint
  • Load balancer health checks misconfigured to POST to application paths
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full request (body if captured) for the flagged /OA_HTML/ibytransmit POST — confirm it originates from an external/untrusted IP and look for a DeliveryRequest XML with CODEX_PULL and FULL_FILE_PATH (e.g. /etc/passwd). Check HTTP status 200 = likely successful file read. 2) Contain: block the source IP at the WAF/perimeter, and if the EBS instance is unpatched (pre May-2026 CPU, versions 12.2.3–12.2.15) take the Payments/File Transmission surface offline or apply the patch immediately. 3) Hunt: on the EBS app host, review UC2 (app-tier shell spawns) and outbound connections from the java/httpd process, and audit for reads of DB credential/config files (context files, wallet, ojdbc creds) that the same actor may have exfiltrated.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where HttpMethod =~ "POST"
| where Url has "ibytransmit"
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstHostname, Url, HttpMethod, HttpStatusCode, HttpRequestBodyBytes, UserAgent = HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

Oracle EBS app-tier (java/httpd) spawning shell or recon binaries post-CVE-2026-46817 AIInstallation Medium
Hunts Oracle E-Business Suite application-tier processes (Oracle HTTP Server httpd, WebLogic/OACORE java) spawning interactive shells, recon utilities, or network tooling — the post-exploitation takeover behaviour following CVE-2026-46817 file-read/RCE on the Payments module. On a hardened EBS app server these parents should rarely spawn ad-hoc shell/recon children. Rationale: CVE-2026-46817's confirmed impact is takeover of the Oracle Payments app tier via the ibytransmit file-read primitive (per Mallory/SoCRadar); the natural follow-on is the web/app-tier daemon (httpd/java) executing shell/recon commands. Parent-child pairing keeps this specific to the compromised EBS host rather than generic shell noise. Cross-checked against: • https://www.mallory.ai/vulnerabilities/CVE-2026-46817 • https://socradar.io/blog/cve-2026-46817-oracle-payments-takeover/ • https://www.theregister.com/cyber-crime/2026/07/02/oracle-e-business-suite-was-under-attack-via-critical-flaw-before-the-public-exploit-code-was-even-released/5265710
ATT&CKT1068 T1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • EBS Concurrent Manager (FNDLIBR) legitimately invoking shell scripts under $APPL_TOP
  • adop / AutoConfig / adpatch maintenance runs spawning sh and perl from the app tier
  • Java managed servers invoking uname/id during startup diagnostics
  • Monitoring agents (OEM/Nagios) launching curl or python health probes from the app account
  • DBA/apps admin interactive troubleshooting on the app tier host
Suppression filter
| where ProcessCommandLine !has "$APPL_TOP" and ProcessCommandLine !has "/appl/" and ProcessCommandLine !has "adop" and ProcessCommandLine !has "FNDLIBR"
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the child ProcessCommandLine and full process ancestry — a genuine EBS job runs a script under $APPL_TOP/$INST_TOP; an interactive whoami/id/uname, a curl/wget to an external IP, or nc listener is not routine. Correlate the timestamp against UC1 ibytransmit hits from the same host. 2) Contain: isolate the EBS app-tier host from the network, suspend the applmgr/apps service account sessions, and snapshot for forensics before reboot. 3) Hunt: search for dropped web shells under OA_HTML/JSP dirs, new/modified cron and systemd units, outbound connections from the java/httpd PID, and reads of context files, Oracle wallet, and ojdbc credential stores.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("java","httpd","apache2")
| where FileName in~ ("bash","sh","dash","whoami","id","uname","curl","wget","nc","ncat","python","python3","perl")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("java","httpd","apache2")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("bash","/sh","dash","whoami","id","uname","curl","wget","/nc","ncat","python","perl")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

Internet-facing hosts exposed to Oracle EBS CVE-2026-46817 (KEV, patch-by 2026-07-18) AIReconnaissance High
Surfaces managed hosts reporting CVE-2026-46817 that are also internet-facing, so the SOC/vuln-mgmt team can prioritise the CISA BOD 26-04 emergency patch deadline. This is an exposure-management pivot on the actively-exploited, KEV-listed Oracle E-Business Suite Payments flaw (affected 12.2.3–12.2.15). Rationale: CVE-2026-46817 is confirmed KEV-listed and actively exploited (CISA BOD 26-04, patch-by 2026-07-18); joining the CVE to IsInternetFacing == true yields the exact assets an unauthenticated internet attacker can reach — the highest-priority remediation list, near-zero FP. Cross-checked against: • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/06/30/oracle-payments-cve-2026-46817-exploitation/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/over-900-oracle-e-business-instances-exposed-to-ongoing-attacks/ • https://socradar.io/blog/cve-2026-46817-oracle-payments-takeover/
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Host already patched with May-2026 CPU but TVM inventory not yet re-scanned (stale vuln record)
  • IsInternetFacing flagged via an upstream NAT/load balancer while the EBS service itself is internally restricted
  • Decommissioned EBS instance still reporting to TVM
  • Non-production/honeypot EBS instance intentionally exposed
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm each host is a live production EBS instance and validate its patch level against the May 2026 Critical Patch Update (versions 12.2.3–12.2.15 are in scope). 2) Contain: if unpatched, apply the CPU or, if patching cannot complete before the 2026-07-18 BOD deadline, restrict the /OA_HTML/ibytransmit surface at the WAF/perimeter and add an emergency deny rule. 3) Hunt: for every exposed host, retro-hunt UC1 web logs for prior /OA_HTML/ibytransmit POSTs and UC2 app-tier shell spawns to rule out pre-patch compromise.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where CveId == "CVE-2026-46817"
| join kind=inner (
    DeviceInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(1d)
    | summarize arg_max(Timestamp, IsInternetFacing, PublicIP) by DeviceId
  ) on DeviceId
| where IsInternetFacing == true
| project DeviceName, DeviceId, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate, PublicIP
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)

Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-46817")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has

// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-46817")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium

| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")

| order by files desc

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] UAT-11795 ClickFix mshta.exe HTA stager fetching from Starland staging domains · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Russian hackers trojanize WebEx, Zoom apps to push Starland malware
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Trojanized WebEx/Zoom/MobaXterm/DBeaver/FACEIT installer spawning Python loader · Suspicious browser extension installation · Scheduled task created with suspicious image / encoded args · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Starland RAT HWID-parameterized C2 / shellcode staging to UAT-11795 domains · [LLM] Starland RAT Polygon smart-contract fallback C2 resolution (eth_call) · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Crypto-wallet file/keystore access by non-wallet process
UAT-11795 ClickFix mshta.exe HTA stager fetching from Starland staging domains AIDelivery High
Hunts mshta.exe launched with a remote HTA URL or one of UAT-11795's staging domains in its command line, matching the campaign's ClickFix initial-access step. This is article-specific because it anchors on mshta reaching eorthopaedics/sastoro/zynaris/web-devtools rather than generic mshta abuse. Rationale: Anchors on mshta.exe (article: 'weaponized HTA downloader via mshta.exe ... likely ClickFix') combined with the six named UAT-11795 staging/C2 domains, so it fires on the specific ClickFix chain rather than generic mshta usage. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/russian-hackers-trojanize-webex-zoom-apps-to-push-starland-malware/
ATT&CKT1218.005 T1204.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legacy line-of-business apps invoking mshta with a local .hta (no http/domain match)
  • IT packaging scripts that fetch an internal HTA over http from an intranet host
  • Security-tool sandbox detonations replaying the same URL
  • Pen-test / red-team ClickFix simulation exercises
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("http://","https://") and ProcessCommandLine has_any (".local","intranet","corp.") and not ProcessCommandLine has_any ("eorthopaedics.com","sastoro.com","zynaris.io","web-devtools.com","aipythondevs.com","windowscreenrepairnearme.com"))
Response runbook
1. Triage: pull the full mshta command line and the parent process; confirm the URL host is one of the six UAT-11795 domains or an unknown external host. 2. Contain: isolate the endpoint, block the staging domains at proxy/DNS, and kill any python.exe/powershell.exe children spawned within 5 min. 3. Hunt: on the same host look for a trojanized installer (WebEx_Client.exe, Zoom, MobaXterm_v26.1.exe, dbeaver-ce-windows-x86_64.exe, FaceitInstaller_x64.exe) drop, python.exe beaconing to api.telegram.org, and subsequent C2 to /feed/ or /alpha/ paths.

Trojanized WebEx/Zoom/MobaXterm/DBeaver/FACEIT installer spawning Python loader AIInstallation High
Hunts UAT-11795's named trojanized installers spawning python.exe/pythonw.exe, which reflects the NSIS-bundled byte-compiled Python loader that decodes Starland RAT in memory. A video-conferencing, DB or SSH installer spawning Python is anomalous and article-specific. Rationale: Uses the exact trojanized-installer filenames listed in the article's lure table plus the python.exe child from the NSIS byte-compiled Python loader description — a collaboration/DB/SSH installer spawning Python is not a legitimate pattern. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/russian-hackers-trojanize-webex-zoom-apps-to-push-starland-malware/

Starland RAT HWID-parameterized C2 / shellcode staging to UAT-11795 domains AICommand & Control High
Hunts host connections or DNS resolutions to UAT-11795's staging and C2 domains carrying the volume-serial HWID URL paths (/feed/, /alpha/) and raw shellcode paths (/starlandfox, /x32remka, /dopfile). Article-specific because it keys on the exact domain+path scheme Starland RAT uses to register victims and pull CastleStealer/Remcos shellcode. Rationale: Every listed domain is a confirmed UAT-11795 staging/C2 host; the /feed/, /alpha/ HWID paths and /starlandfox, /x32remka, /dopfile shellcode paths are unique campaign artifacts, so any resolution/connection is high-fidelity with near-zero legitimate overlap. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/russian-hackers-trojanize-webex-zoom-apps-to-push-starland-malware/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1105 T1132.001

  • Passive DNS collectors or SOAR playbooks pinging the domains for takedown verification
  • DNS sinkhole redirecting these domains, generating benign resolution logs

1. Contain: isolate the host, sinkhole/block all six domains, and capture memory before reboot (Starland decodes in memory). 3. Hunt: pivot on the volume-serial HWID string as the final URL path component across the estate, check for Polygon RPC fallback resolution (contract 0x6ae382ed2154cc84c6672e4e908cd2c69c1b35ba), and Telegram beacons to bots 8384531459/7993597060.

Starland RAT Polygon smart-contract fallback C2 resolution (eth_call) AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts the Starland RAT / mshta / PowerShell interpreters reaching Polygon (MATIC) public JSON-RPC endpoints, the backup C2-resolution channel that reads an XOR-encrypted fallback domain from smart contract 0x6ae382ed2154cc84c6672e4e908cd2c69c1b35ba via eth_call. Article-specific because legitimate endpoints rarely query Polygon RPC from a scripting interpreter. Rationale: Article states Starland RAT resolves fallback C2 via eth_call to Polygon contract 0x6ae382ed2154cc84c6672e4e908cd2c69c1b35ba; scoping Polygon RPC egress to scripting interpreters (not a browser or wallet app) isolates the RAT's blockchain-DGA behavior. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/russian-hackers-trojanize-webex-zoom-apps-to-push-starland-malware/

  • Blockchain data-analytics jobs on a workstation
  • Security researcher reproducing the eth_call to inspect the contract
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\AppData\Local\Temp\", @"\Downloads\", @"\AppData\Roaming\") or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe")
Response runbook
1. Triage: confirm the initiating interpreter and its parent — a python.exe under a trojanized-installer tree hitting Polygon RPC is the RAT; a standalone dev script is likely benign. 2. Contain: isolate the host, block the Polygon RPC hosts for that endpoint, and capture memory to recover the decrypted fallback C2 domain. 3. Hunt: extract the resolved fallback domain and sweep the estate for it; correlate with contacts to the six primary domains and Telegram bot beacons; look for CastleStealer .NET stealer and Remcos artifacts.

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
Network connections to article IPs / domains Command & Control High
Outbound traffic to attacker infrastructure named in the article.
ATT&CKT1071
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web Network_Resolution.DNS DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteIP in ("") or RemoteUrl has_any ("eorthopaedics.com", "sastoro.com", "web-devtools.com", "zynaris.io", "windowscreenrepairnearme.com", "aipythondevs.com")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
let BadIPs     = dynamic([""]);
let BadDomains = dynamic(["eorthopaedics.com", "sastoro.com", "web-devtools.com", "zynaris.io", "windowscreenrepairnearme.com", "aipythondevs.com"]);
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DstIpAddr in (BadIPs)
   or Url has_any (BadDomains)
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, Url, NetworkProtocol
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.
ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType

// ASIM ImFileEvent — covers MDE, Sysmon, AuditD, Defender for Cloud, etc.
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\",
                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",
                                  @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName,
          TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d06
status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1204.002
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\explorer.exe'
            - '\RuntimeBroker.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
    selection_cmd:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'iex'
            - 'invoke-expression'
            - 'frombase64'
            - 'downloadstring'
            - 'hxxp'
            - 'curl '
            - 'wget '
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_cmd
falsepositives:
    - IT-driven scripted automation that admins paste-launch
level: high
ENDPOINT

      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
